t: Early pregnancy: ectopic, pregnancy loss and trophoblastic disease
sub: A four-question framework, pregnant, intrauterine, viable, stable, that sorts first-trimester bleeding into normal pregnancy, loss, ectopic pregnancy or molar disease.

pretest.q: A woman with a positive pregnancy test has a serum hCG of 4,000 mIU/mL and no intrauterine sac on transvaginal ultrasound. What is the main concern?
pretest.why: Above the discriminatory level, about 3,500 mIU/mL, a normal intrauterine gestational sac should be visible on transvaginal ultrasound, so an empty uterus means ectopic pregnancy until proven otherwise; a completed miscarriage is the main alternative.

w.Normal early intrauterine pregnancy: A normal pregnancy this far along should already show a gestational sac; too early to see is plausible only below the discriminatory level.
w.Complete molar pregnancy: A complete mole fills the uterus with heterogeneous cystic tissue, the snowstorm pattern, so the cavity would not look empty.
w.Threatened abortion: Threatened abortion requires a visible intrauterine pregnancy with a closed os; here no intrauterine pregnancy has been seen at all.

pretest.q: Which karyotype is typical of a complete hydatidiform mole?
o: 46,XX, one maternal and one paternal set
pretest.why: An empty ovum with no maternal chromosomes is fertilized by one sperm that duplicates its DNA, or less often by two sperm, so every chromosome is paternal; without maternal genes no fetus forms.

w.69,XXY, two paternal sets: Triploidy from a normal egg fertilized by two sperm is the partial mole, which has fetal parts and a lower hCG.
w.46,XX, one maternal and one paternal set: A biparental diploid karyotype is a normal conceptus; a complete mole has lost every maternal chromosome.
w.45,X, maternal: Monosomy X is Turner syndrome, a common chromosomal cause of early pregnancy loss with cystic hygroma, not a molar pregnancy.

pretest.q: A woman at 9 weeks has bleeding, a closed cervical os and an embryo with cardiac activity. What is the diagnosis?
pretest.why: Bleeding with a closed os and a live intrauterine embryo is a threatened abortion; most of these pregnancies continue, and management is expectant.

w.Inevitable abortion: Inevitable abortion means the internal os has opened with the products still inside; loss cannot be stopped once the cervix dilates.
w.Missed abortion: A missed abortion is a nonviable pregnancy with no cardiac activity, retained behind a closed os, often with little or no bleeding.
w.Incomplete abortion: Incomplete abortion means some tissue has passed through an open os and some remains, so bleeding and cramping continue.

body: How do you work through bleeding or pain in early pregnancy?

Every patient with bleeding or pain in early pregnancy is sorted by four questions asked in order. Is she pregnant? A urine or serum **pregnancy test** detects human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG), which proves that trophoblast exists somewhere but not where. Is the pregnancy intrauterine? Transvaginal ultrasound answers that. Is it viable? Cardiac activity and a rising hCG trend answer that. Is she stable? Syncope, shoulder pain, severe pain or **hemodynamic instability** means possible rupture and internal bleeding, which comes before every other step. Pain plus bleeding plus a positive test without a confirmed intrauterine pregnancy is an **ectopic** pregnancy until proven otherwise, and every Rh-negative woman who bleeds receives anti-D immune globulin.

Transvaginal ultrasound shows a predictable sequence. A **gestational sac** appears at about 5 weeks, a **yolk sac** at 5 to 6 weeks, a **fetal pole** at about 6 weeks, and cardiac activity at 6 to 7 weeks. Because a fluid collection in an ectopic pregnancy can mimic a sac, the yolk sac is the first definite sign of an intrauterine pregnancy. Gestational age is counted from the first day of the last menstrual period, so it runs about 2 weeks ahead of fetal age; when dates are uncertain, the embryo's crown-rump length gives the most accurate first-trimester dating.

The hCG number is read against the ultrasound. The {{rp26_dz|discriminatory zone}} is the hCG level above which a normal intrauterine sac should be visible; current guidance uses a level as high as 3,500 mIU/mL so that a wanted pregnancy is never treated as ectopic too early. An empty uterus above that level suggests ectopic pregnancy or a completed loss. Below it, an empty uterus is a {{rp26_pul|pregnancy of unknown location}}, resolved with **serial** hCG measurements 48 hours apart and repeat imaging: a viable intrauterine pregnancy usually rises at least about 35 percent, a failing pregnancy falls, and an ectopic often rises slowly or plateaus.
Fluid sac in the uterus; a pseudosac can mimic it
First definite sign of an intrauterine pregnancy
The embryo; its crown-rump length dates the pregnancy
Viability; none at a crown-rump length of 7 mm or more means loss
Empty uterus with hCG above about 3,500
Ectopic pregnancy or completed loss until proven otherwise
One hCG value cannot locate a pregnancy

A single hCG proves only that trophoblast exists. Location needs ultrasound, and viability needs a trend over 48 hours, so treating on one number risks giving methotrexate to a wanted, normal pregnancy or sending home a woman whose ectopic is still growing. Follow the patient, not the number: pain, instability or free fluid override any hCG value.
Why is ectopic pregnancy the diagnosis you cannot miss?

A fertilized egg normally reaches the uterus about 5 days after ovulation, so anything that slows tubal transport lets it implant in the tube. The biggest risk is tubal scarring and ciliary damage from **pelvic inflammatory disease**, usually chlamydial; others are a prior ectopic, tubal surgery, smoking, infertility treatment and conception with an IUD in place. About 1 to 2 percent of pregnancies are ectopic, and most implant in the **ampulla** of the uterine tube. The tube cannot expand like the uterus, so trophoblast erodes its wall and vessels, and **rupture** causes hemoperitoneum, the leading cause of first-trimester maternal death.

The classic picture is amenorrhea, abdominal pain and vaginal bleeding with a tender adnexal mass, an empty uterus and an hCG that rises slowly. Shoulder pain means blood irritating the diaphragm, and hypotension with peritoneal signs means rupture, so an unstable patient goes straight to surgery, usually laparoscopic salpingectomy. A stable patient with an unruptured ectopic, no embryonic cardiac activity, a modest hCG (commonly below about 5,000 mIU/mL) and reliable follow-up can receive intramuscular **methotrexate**, a folate antagonist that inhibits dihydrofolate reductase and kills dividing trophoblast. Her hCG must then fall at least 15 percent between days 4 and 7 and be followed to zero.
How do the types of pregnancy loss differ?

Early pregnancy loss ends about 10 to 20 percent of recognized pregnancies, and at least half of first-trimester losses are caused by fetal chromosomal abnormalities, mostly autosomal trisomies, not by exercise, sex or stress. Each type is named from two findings: whether the cervical os is open and whether tissue has passed. A **threatened** abortion is bleeding with a closed os and a live embryo, and most continue. An **inevitable** abortion has an open os with the products still inside. Incomplete means some tissue has passed, complete means the uterus is empty, and a **missed** abortion is a nonviable pregnancy retained behind a closed os.
Nonviable embryo or empty sac retained
Recurrent loss has a short list of causes

Two or more losses call for a search for treatable causes. {{rp26_apls|Antiphospholipid syndrome}} causes placental thrombosis and is treated with low-dose aspirin plus heparin. A **septate uterus** gives the embryo a poorly vascularized implantation site and can be resected. A parental **balanced translocation**, found by karyotyping both partners, produces unbalanced embryos. Uncontrolled diabetes and thyroid disease complete the list of **recurrent** loss causes.
What makes a pregnancy molar, and when does it become cancer?

A hydatidiform mole is a conception whose trophoblast overgrows because it carries too many paternal chromosomes. In a **complete mole**, an ovum that has lost its own nucleus is fertilized by one sperm that duplicates, giving 46,XX with every chromosome **paternal**, or less often by two sperm. With no maternal genes, no embryo forms, and every villus swells into a grape-like vesicle ringed by proliferating trophoblast. In a **partial mole**, a normal ovum is fertilized by two sperm, giving a triploid 69,XXY karyotype; the maternal set allows fetal parts to form, but the fetus is abnormal and not viable.
Paternal genes build placenta; maternal genes build the embryo

Genomic imprinting explains the pattern. Paternally expressed genes drive trophoblast growth, while maternally expressed genes such as p57 are needed for the embryo. A complete mole, with only paternal chromosomes, grows trophoblast and no fetus and is negative on the {{rp26_p57|p57 immunostain}}; a partial mole keeps one maternal set, so fetal parts form and villous cells stain positive.

Very high hCG produces most of the clinical clues. Women present with vaginal bleeding or passage of grape-like tissue, a uterus large for dates, **hyperemesis** gravidarum, preeclampsia before 20 weeks, theca lutein ovarian cysts and sometimes hyperthyroidism. Ultrasound of a complete mole shows a **snowstorm** or cluster of grapes pattern with no fetus. Risk is highest at the extremes of **maternal age**, teenagers and especially women over 40, and after a prior mole: one prior molar pregnancy raises the risk of another to about 1 to 2 percent. Nulliparity and Asian ancestry also add risk.
Managing a molar pregnancy, in order
Baseline hCG, blood count, blood type and Rh, coagulation, liver, kidney and thyroid tests and a chest x-ray come first, because a molar uterus can hemorrhage.
Suction curettage empties the uterus; medical evacuation is avoided because it bleeds more and leaves more persistent disease, and hysterectomy suits women who want no more children.
Serial hCG follow-up measures the hCG level weekly until undetectable and then monthly for several months, and Rh-negative women receive anti-D immune globulin.
Reliable hormonal contraception keeps a new pregnancy from raising hCG and hiding a recurrence; a plateau or rise means neoplasia and chemotherapy.

A plateau or rise in hCG after evacuation defines {{rp26_gtn|gestational trophoblastic neoplasia}}, which follows about 15 to 20 percent of complete moles but under 5 percent of partial moles. An **invasive mole** has molar villi burrowing into the myometrium and rarely spreads. **Choriocarcinoma** has sheets of cytotrophoblast and syncytiotrophoblast with no villi, invades vessels early and metastasizes by blood to the lungs, vagina, brain and liver; it can follow a mole, a miscarriage, an ectopic or a term delivery. A **placental site** trophoblastic tumor arises from intermediate trophoblast, makes hPL with little hCG and resists chemotherapy, so it is treated by hysterectomy. The other gestational tumors respond dramatically to methotrexate or actinomycin D, even when metastatic.
Focal cystic placenta with a fetus
Suspected mole, uterus large for dates

body.q: After evacuation of a complete mole, a woman's hCG falls for 4 weeks and then stays flat for 3 weeks. Which reasoning is best?
o: A plateau is normal laboratory variation, so hCG can be rechecked in 6 months once she stops contraception
A plateau means she has conceived again, so an ultrasound should look for a new intrauterine pregnancy
A plateau means only that some tissue was left behind, so a repeat curettage will always cure her
A plateau means trophoblast is persisting and growing, so it is gestational trophoblastic neoplasia and needs staging and chemotherapy
body.why: After a complete evacuation, hCG should fall steadily to undetectable. A plateau over three weeks or a rise means trophoblast is surviving and dividing, which defines gestational trophoblastic neoplasia; she needs staging, including a chest x-ray for lung metastases, and usually single-agent methotrexate or actinomycin D, which cures most low-risk disease. Contraception during follow-up exists precisely so that a new pregnancy cannot be confused with persistent disease, and repeat curettage alone does not reliably treat trophoblast that has invaded the myometrium.

body: Why can a molar pregnancy cause hyperthyroidism and severe vomiting?

Both come from the enormous hCG output of proliferating trophoblast, often well over 100,000 mIU/mL and far higher than in a normal pregnancy. hCG shares its alpha subunit with TSH, LH and FSH, and its beta subunit resembles TSH's closely enough that, at these levels, it activates the TSH receptor, so free T4 rises and TSH falls. The same excess drives hyperemesis gravidarum, whose vomiting causes weight loss, ketosis and a hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis, and it overstimulates ovarian LH receptors to form theca lutein cysts. Evacuating the mole removes the trophoblast, hCG falls, and all three problems resolve.

grid.q: Which findings point to a complete hydatidiform mole?
items: Adnexal mass with an empty uterus
hCG rising less than 35 percent in 48 hours
